title: Environment Variable Permissions
summary: Environment variable permissions control who may read or change the variables that processes inherit at start-up, because those variables carry search paths, configuration locations, proxy settings and sometimes secrets. The mechanism is ordinary file and registry access control: on Unix-like systems the profile scripts, service unit files and configuration under system directories are made writable only by the root account, while on Windows the machine and user environment keys and the startup locations that define them are restricted to administrators and the system account. Real environments enforce it through hardening baselines, service manager hardening directives, container image policies that forbid writable privileged paths, and configuration management of service definitions rather than hand edits on live hosts. Evidence appears in file and registry auditing, change tracking on profile and unit files, and process environment data collected during incident response, which frequently shows how a service was redirected to load an attacker-supplied file. The common misunderstanding is that environment variables are harmless text; a writable directory early in a search path, or an inherited library path, lets an attacker choose which code a privileged process loads.

beginner.definition: Environment variables are small settings that a program reads when it starts. They can point to where files live, or how a program should connect to the network. Environment variable permissions decide who is allowed to change those settings.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker can change these settings, they can quietly redirect a trusted program. The program may then load a harmful file instead of the real one. This can happen without any software exploit, because the program simply trusts its own settings. Locking the settings down removes that easy path completely.
howItWorks: Programs read environment variables at the exact moment they start running on the system.
Those variables often name the folders a program searches for libraries or tools.
If a normal user can change them, an attacker can point them somewhere else.
The operating system then loads the attacker's file instead of the real one.
Locking the settings down to administrators only closes this path for good.
beginner.example: Think of a delivery driver who follows written directions to a warehouse. If somebody can swap the note on the dashboard, the driver will happily deliver the parcel to the wrong address. The driver did nothing wrong and broke no rule. Environment variable permissions are the locked glovebox that stops anyone from swapping the note in the first place.
takeaways: Settings that a program trusts are part of your attack surface, not just configuration.
Only administrators should change system wide environment variables and search paths.
Audit changes to profile, service and start-up files, because they show this abuse clearly.

objectives: Explain how environment variables influence which code a process loads.
Identify the Unix and Windows locations where these settings are defined.
Describe how a writable search path leads to code execution without an exploit.
Apply least privilege to profile scripts, service definitions and registry keys.
Use process environment data during incident response and root cause analysis.
